case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. (FR) Application No. 777/96, decided on 31 March 2000

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the appointments of Jayawardena and Ziyard to the post of Deputy Chief Legal Officer and Supernumerary Deputy Chief Legal Officer respectively infringed the fundamental right to equality guaranteed by Article 12(1) of the Constitution, and whether the application challenging these appointments was time-barred or misconceived.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that the selection process for the post of Deputy Chief Legal Officer was arbitrary, discriminatory, and lacked rational criteria, infringing Article 12(1). He challenged the appointments of Jayawardena and Ziyard, seeking cancellation of their appointments.
case_context.respondent_argument: Respondents argued that the application challenging Jayawardena's appointment was time-barred as it was filed well beyond the one-month period prescribed by Article 126(2). Regarding Ziyard's appointment as Supernumerary Deputy Chief Legal Officer, it was contended that the appointment was a result of a court settlement and effectively a retiral benefit, not an executive or administrative action infringing Article 12(1).
key_facts: Four officers (Narendrakumar, Ziyard, Jayawardena, Kiritharan) were eligible for the Deputy Chief Legal Officer post.
Jayawardena was selected and appointed effective 1.8.1995; her appointment was challenged by Ziyard within one month.
Ziyard later reached optional retirement age; was appointed Supernumerary Deputy Chief Legal Officer via court settlement on 23.10.1996.
Petitioner filed the present application on 25.11.1996 challenging both appointments.
The application against Jayawardena's appointment was filed well beyond the one-month time limit.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court interpreted Article 12(1) as guaranteeing equality before the law and equal protection, requiring classification to be based on intelligible differentia with rational relation to the objective. The right to apply for constitutional redress under Article 126(2) is personal and must be exercised within one month of the infringement or knowledge thereof. Delay without adequate excuse results in dismissal. The Court distinguished between actual and imminent infringements and emphasized the individual nature of the right to apply.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found the petitioner's challenge to Jayawardena's appointment was time-barred as it was filed more than one month after the appointment was known. The petitioner could not rely on Ziyard's earlier timely application as the right to apply is personal and cannot be delegated or delayed. Regarding Ziyard's appointment, the Court held it was a court settlement conferring retiral benefits, not an executive or administrative appointment infringing Article 12(1). The petitioner was not similarly situated to Ziyard and thus could not claim infringement.
principles_established: The right to equality under Article 12(1) requires rational classification.
The right to apply for fundamental rights enforcement under Article 126(2) is personal and time-bound.
Court settlements conferring retiral benefits do not constitute executive or administrative action infringing fundamental rights.
Delay in filing fundamental rights applications without adequate excuse leads to dismissal.
precedents_cited: Gunawardena v. Senanayake FRD Vol. 1 p. 177
Jayawardena v. Attorney-General FRD Vol. 1 p. 175
Krishna Mining Co. Ltd. v. JEDB (1996) 2 SRI LR. 209
Gamacthige v. Sirimardena and others (1998) 1 SRI LR. 384

outcome.holding: The Court upheld the preliminary objections and dismissed the application. The challenge to Jayawardena's appointment was dismissed as time-barred, and the challenge to Ziyard's appointment was dismissed as misconceived.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the petitioner's claim of discrimination and arbitrariness in the appointment process. The Court's reasoning on the personal and time-bound nature of the right to equality and its enforcement under Article 126(2) directly influenced the dismissal of the application.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court held that the right to apply under Article 126(2) is personal and must be exercised within one month of the infringement. The petitioner’s delay in challenging Jayawardena’s appointment was fatal. The appointment of Ziyard was a court settlement conferring retiral benefits, not an infringement of Article 12(1).
